verses.text: If I speak with the languages of men and of angels, but don’t have love, I have become sounding brass, or a clanging cymbal.
If I have the gift of prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge; and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but don’t have love, I am nothing.
If I dole out all my goods to feed the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but don’t have love, it profits me nothing.
Love is patient and is kind; love doesn’t envy. Love doesn’t brag, is not proud,
doesn’t behave itself inappropriately, doesn’t seek its own way, is not provoked, takes no account of evil;
doesn’t rejoice in unrighteousness, but rejoices with the truth;
bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.
Love never fails. But where there are prophecies, they will be done away with. Where there are various languages, they will cease. Where there is knowledge, it will be done away with.
For we know in part, and we prophesy in part;
but when that which is complete has come, then that which is partial will be done away with.
When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I felt as a child, I thought as a child. Now that I have become a man, I have put away childish things.
For now we see in a mirror, dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I will know fully, even as I was also fully known.
But now faith, hope, and love remain — these three. The greatest of these is love.

footnotes.content: Even the most beautiful eloquence — the words that move crowds and turn heads — becomes mere noise without love underneath. Paul knew this from the inside: he had both the gift of speech and the fire of passion, yet he's telling us that without love, all that gift becomes hollow percussion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To know all mysteries and move mountains — what power, what achievement — yet to be nothing without love. I've seen clever, capable people burn themselves out proving their worth, when all along the Lord was waiting for their heart to soften and turn toward others.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul knows the cost — "I give my body to be burned." The Roman fires, the martyrs' pyre. Yet even sacrifice without love profits nothing. He's telling us that heroic generosity divorced from genuine care becomes a kind of vanity, a performance for the watching world rather than a gift born of the heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Patient, kind, no envy, no bragging, not proud — these are the opening notes of love's true melody. What Paul is describing isn't a feeling but a posture: a way of showing up for someone else without calculating what we get in return. It's the way Jesus looked at us while we were still stumbling.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Love doesn't keep score, doesn't blow up, doesn't rehearse old wounds. I've watched long marriages work because two people chose not to count every slight, but instead to bear with each other the way Christ bears with us — holding our failures without throwing them back in our face.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Love doesn't gloat when someone stumbles, doesn't secretly celebrate another's downfall — even when they maybe deserved it. Instead, love finds its joy in what is true and good and lasting. That's a hard habit to break, and yet it's the mark of a heart being shaped by Christ.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things." Paul piles on the "alls" — there's a generosity here, a refusal to give up on someone. This is how the Father loved us: bearing with us when we were foolish, believing we could change, hoping for us before we hoped for ourselves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Prophecies will fade, languages will cease, knowledge will pass away — all the things we thought were permanent and important. But love never fails. It outlasts every gift, every advantage, every certainty we cling to. Only love remains when everything else crumbles.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "We know in part" — there's humility in this. We don't have it all figured out, and that's okay. Our knowledge is fractured, our sight is limited, our prophecies are incomplete. But somehow, knowing this — admitting it — opens us to something truer than all our certainties put together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When the whole comes, the fragments will fade. Paul is pointing us forward, past the fog of this life, to a day when we won't need guesses anymore. Until then, we live by partial sight and partial love — but that partial love is real, and it's enough.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Growing up means putting away childish ways — but not joy, not wonder, not trust. It means learning to think beyond yourself, to see others, to understand that the world doesn't exist to serve you. That's the maturity Christ calls us toward: not hardness, but wisdom; not control, but love.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this verse: we see through screens and mirrors still, dimly, fragments. Yet Paul reminds us that one day — and he believed it was soon — we will see face to face, known fully as we are known. Even now, that promise reaches across centuries and tells us our fumbling is temporary, and love is eternal. As of 2026-10, I hold onto that.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Faith and hope are precious — they hold us through the night. But Paul gives the crown to love. It will outlast faith (when we see, we won't need to believe anymore) and outlast hope (when we have what we hoped for, we won't need to hope). Love alone is eternal.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
